waypoints.name: SR-20 Hairpin Pullout
waypoints.note: Large paved pullout at the hairpin turn on the North Cascades Highway just east of Washington Pass crest; no signed trailhead — find the boot path into the timber/boulder field on the uphill side. Northwest Forest Pass required.
waypoints.directions: Drive the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) to the first hairpin turn about a mile east of the Washington Pass summit and park in the large paved turnout on the south side of the road, around 5,160 ft. Nothing here is signed as a trailhead; the boot path starts on the uphill side of the pullout, into the timber and boulders. SR-20 is gated for winter from roughly early December to mid or late April, so check the WSDOT pass report in the shoulder seasons, and display a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass.

waypoints.name: Boulder Field / Snowline
waypoints.note: Cairns mark the climbers' path up through timber and talus to about 5,800 ft, where the route commonly meets lingering snowpack well into summer.
waypoints.directions: From the pullout head south and southeast toward the foot of the large talus slope just south of Spire Gulch, below the north side of Kangaroo Temple. Pick up the boot path skirting the bottom of the talus and follow the cairns carefully: this lower boulder and talus band is the trickiest route-finding on the whole approach, and it is considerably worse when snow covers the tread early in the season. Around 5,800 ft you reach the level where snowpack commonly lingers well into summer.

waypoints.name: Kangaroo Pass
waypoints.note: Gain the crest of Kangaroo Ridge here between Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak, about 1,500 ft above the trailhead; leave the approach path and turn east onto Wallaby's southwest ridge.
waypoints.directions: Above the boulder band the tread firms up into a distinct, easy-to-follow cairned trail through the upper basin. Keep climbing mixed talus, boulders and open slope to the crest of Kangaroo Ridge at Kangaroo Pass, 6,671 ft, roughly 1,500 ft of gain from the car in about 1 to 1.5 hours. A small tarn just below the pass is the only water on the route and can be dry by late summer or fall; there is none higher, so carry enough from the car. Expect snow on this stretch into early or mid summer depending on the year, and carry an ice axe or microspikes into July.

waypoints.name: 7,400 ft Ridge-to-Face Swing
waypoints.note: The southwest ridge narrows here; step off the crest and traverse onto the south-facing flank to reach the summit gully — boot tracks are sparse and easy to lose in poor visibility.
waypoints.directions: Leave the boot path at the pass and gain Wallaby's southwest ridge. A faint climbers' trail runs a short way and then disappears on rock, so the rest is route-finding: stay on or near the crest, weaving between its north and south sides across mixed rock, scree and grassy benches, about 530 ft of gain to an access notch near 7,200 ft. The short section between that notch and about 7,400 ft is the technical crux of the route and holds a corniced snow arete into late spring, where an axe and light crampons are commonly used.

waypoints.name: South-Facing Summit Gully
waypoints.note: Loose talus and scree gully gains the final several hundred feet; Class 3 rock on either side avoids the worst scree, and this same gully is the descent line — watch for rockfall from parties above.
waypoints.directions: Where the crest narrows near 7,400 ft, step off it and traverse onto the south-facing flank to reach the summit gully. Boot tracks are sparse here and easy to lose in poor visibility. The gully is moderately steep with a great deal of loose rock and scree, so wear a helmet and avoid stacking the party directly above one another, since anyone higher will kick debris onto anyone below. Many parties take a short Class 3 line on the more solid rock at the gully's margins rather than wading up the scree.

waypoints.name: Wallaby Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Wallaby Peak on Kangaroo Ridge (7,995 ft); first climbed by Fred and Helmy Beckey with Walt Varney on June 17, 1942.
waypoints.directions: Climb the gully for the final several hundred feet, then near its top exit left, to the northeast, for the short scramble to the true summit at 7,995 ft. The slabs just below the summit block stay exposed and are genuinely committing when wet or snow-covered, even in midsummer. This same gully is the descent line, downclimbed one at a time.

access.fees: No fee at the informal SR-20 turnout; a Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass is commonly displayed there and is required at developed trailheads in the district
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.permit: No permit required for day scrambling; the upper route brushes the boundary of the adjoining Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness
access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) is gated for winter, typically closing in early December and reopening mid-to-late April at Washington Pass and Rainy Pass depending on snowpack and avalanche hazard — the peak is inaccessible by car during that window; check WSDOT mountain pass reports before a shoulder-season trip
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District — 24 West Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA; (509) 996-4000
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful pass recommended

overnight_permit.where: Dispersed camping on National Forest land is free; nearby developed campgrounds charge a site fee and take no reservation.

pro_tips: Start early from Home Lake to be off the couloir/summit before afternoon thunderstorms build and before the snow softens.
Most parties treat this as a 2-day trip with a camp at Home Lake, given the roughly 9.3-mile, ~4,800 ft one-way approach to the base of the route.
Look for Fred Beckey's name, reportedly carved into rock at the saddle between Warrior's twin summits during his 1945 first ascent.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Long approach (~9-10 miles one-way to Home Lake/Constance Pass with ~4,000-5,000 ft of gain); most parties treat it as a 2-day trip with a camp at Home Lake, though fit/fast parties occasionally push it in a day
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight pack (roughly 30-40+ lbs) typical for the standard 2-day itinerary, including rope, rack, and camping gear; day-trip attempts require a much lighter, faster-and-lighter kit and a strong pace

partner_requirements.approachTime: Typically a 2-day trip: day 1 hikes in ~9 miles to a camp near Home Lake/Constance Pass, day 2 climbs the gullies/ledges to the Southeast summit and returns; strong parties have day-tripped it but this is not the norm
requiredSkills: Comfortable free-climbing exposed low-5th-class terrain on poor-quality Olympic rock
Belayed climbing with a single rope for the crux steps below/above the saddle
Basic snow/ice axe skills for lingering couloir snow, especially early in the season
Off-trail route-finding and navigation to correctly identify the (higher) Southeast summit vs. the Northwest summit
Rockfall awareness and loose-rock management, particularly in gullies
Self-sufficiency for a remote, multi-day approach far from rescue access
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced scrambler / intermediate alpine climber - not a beginner objective. The Mountaineers classify this as a Basic Alpine Climb; partners should be comfortable on exposed, loose, low-5th-class rock far from help
